# Introduction

Home-court advantage is one of the most consistent patterns in sports: NBA home teams
historically win roughly 58–60% of games. But *why* home teams win is debated. Possible
explanations include crowd support, referee bias influenced by crowds, travel fatigue
for the visiting team, and familiarity with the arena.

The COVID-19 pandemic created a **natural experiment**. From July to October 2020 the NBA
finished its season in a "bubble" at a neutral site with no fans, and for much of the
2020–21 season teams played in their own arenas with no or limited fans. This lets us
separate the effect of **crowds** from the effect of **travel and familiarity**.

**Research questions**

1. Was the home team's winning percentage lower in games played without fans?
2. Does this difference remain after controlling for the relative strength of the two teams?
3. Does playing in the home arena *without* fans still give an advantage, compared with the neutral-site bubble?

This question matters beyond basketball trivia. If fans are the main source of home-court
advantage, then crowds have a measurable effect on game outcomes, which is relevant for
sports betting models, ticket pricing, and how leagues think about scheduling and referee training.

# Data

```{r load}
games <- read_csv("data/nba_games_2015_2025.csv")
```

The data come from ESPN via the `hoopR` R package and cover all completed regular-season and
playoff games from the 2014–15 season through the 2024–25 season
(**`r format(nrow(games), big.mark = ",")` games**). Each row is one game, with the home and away
teams, final scores, and reported attendance.

## Defining the crowd condition

```{r clean}
games <- games |>
  mutate(
    home_win = as.integer(home_score > away_score),
    margin   = home_score - away_score,           # home point margin
    bubble   = venue == "ESPN Wide World of Sports Complex",
    crowd = case_when(
      bubble                                   ~ "Bubble (neutral, no fans)",
      season == 2021 & attendance == 0         ~ "Home arena, no fans",
      season == 2021 & attendance < 10000      ~ "Limited fans",
      TRUE                                     ~ "Full crowd"
    ),
    crowd = factor(crowd, levels = c("Full crowd", "Limited fans",
                                     "Home arena, no fans", "Bubble (neutral, no fans)")),
    playoffs = season_type == "Playoffs"
  )

games |> count(crowd) |> knitr::kable(col.names = c("Crowd condition", "Games"))
```

- **Bubble**: all games at the Orlando bubble (July–October 2020). Neither team is really "at home".
- **Home arena, no fans**: 2020–21 season games with reported attendance of zero.
- **Limited fans**: 2020–21 games with between 1 and 9,999 fans.
- **Full crowd**: all other games.

A small number of zero-attendance games outside 2020–21 are likely data-entry errors and are
treated as full-crowd games.

## Controlling for team strength

Better teams win more often regardless of location, so we need a measure of team quality.
For each team-season we compute the team's overall regular-season winning percentage, and
define `strength_diff` = home team win% − away team win%.

```{r strength}
team_season <- games |>
  filter(season_type == "Regular") |>
  select(season, home_team, away_team, home_win) |>
  pivot_longer(c(home_team, away_team), names_to = "side", values_to = "team") |>
  mutate(win = if_else(side == "home_team", home_win, 1L - home_win)) |>
  group_by(season, team) |>
  summarise(win_pct = mean(win), .groups = "drop")

games <- games |>
  left_join(team_season, by = c("season", "home_team" = "team")) |>
  rename(home_wpct = win_pct) |>
  left_join(team_season, by = c("season", "away_team" = "team")) |>
  rename(away_wpct = win_pct) |>
  mutate(strength_diff = home_wpct - away_wpct)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

## Home win percentage by season

```{r eda-season}
games |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(home_win_pct = mean(home_win), n = n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(season, home_win_pct)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1d428a") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2019.6, xmax = 2021.4, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           alpha = 0.1, fill = "orange") +
  annotate("text", x = 2020.5, y = 0.62, label = "COVID seasons", size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2025) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.45, 0.65)) +
  labs(x = "Season (ending year)", y = "Home win %",
       title = "Home team winning percentage by season")
```

```{r era}
era <- games |>
  mutate(era = case_when(season <= 2019 ~ "Pre-COVID (2015–2019)",
                         season >= 2022 ~ "Post-COVID (2022–2025)",
                         TRUE           ~ "COVID (2020–2021)")) |>
  group_by(era) |>
  summarise(home_win_pct = mean(home_win), games = n())
pre_pct  <- era$home_win_pct[era$era == "Pre-COVID (2015–2019)"]
post_pct <- era$home_win_pct[era$era == "Post-COVID (2022–2025)"]
```

Before COVID, home teams won about `r scales::percent(pre_pct, 0.1)` of games. The rate
dropped during the 2020 and 2021 seasons, but it did **not** fully bounce back once fans
returned: from 2022 to 2025 home teams won only `r scales::percent(post_pct, 0.1)` of games.
This suggests home-court advantage was already shrinking for reasons unrelated to COVID
(for example, better travel and sleep management, or more three-point shooting, which adds
randomness). We keep this trend in mind when interpreting the no-fan effect.

## Home win percentage and point margin by crowd condition

```{r eda-crowd}
crowd_summary <- games |>
  group_by(crowd) |>
  summarise(
    games        = n(),
    home_win_pct = mean(home_win),
    se           = sqrt(home_win_pct * (1 - home_win_pct) / games),
    avg_margin   = mean(margin)
  )

crowd_summary |>
  mutate(home_win_pct = scales::percent(home_win_pct, 0.1),
         se = round(se, 3), avg_margin = round(avg_margin, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Crowd", "Games", "Home win %", "SE", "Avg home margin"))

ggplot(crowd_summary, aes(crowd, home_win_pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1d428a", width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = home_win_pct - 1.96 * se, ymax = home_win_pct + 1.96 * se),
                width = 0.15) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.35, 0.65)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Home win % (95% CI)",
       title = "Home win percentage by crowd condition")
```

## Distribution of home point margin

```{r eda-margin}
games |>
  filter(crowd %in% c("Full crowd", "Home arena, no fans")) |>
  ggplot(aes(margin, fill = crowd)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Home score − away score", y = "Density", fill = NULL,
       title = "Home point margin: full crowd vs. no fans") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Both distributions are roughly bell-shaped and have similar spreads (SD of about
`r round(sd(games$margin[games$crowd == "Full crowd"]), 1)` points with a full crowd and
`r round(sd(games$margin[games$crowd == "Home arena, no fans"]), 1)` without fans).
The no-fan curve is shifted slightly to the left, meaning home teams won by fewer points.
The shift is small compared with the overall spread, so any single game is still very
unpredictable. Since the samples are large and the shapes are close to normal, a t-test
is appropriate here.

# Methods

1. **Two-proportion z-test**: compare the home win rate in full-crowd games vs. no-fan games.
2. **Welch two-sample t-test**: compare the average home point margin.
3. **Logistic regression**: model the probability of a home win as a function of crowd
   condition, controlling for team strength difference and playoff games.
4. **Linear regression**: model the home point margin with the same predictors, as a robustness check.

# Results

## Hypothesis tests

**H₀:** the home win probability is the same with and without fans.
**H₁:** the home win probability is different.

```{r prop-test}
full   <- games |> filter(crowd == "Full crowd")
nofans <- games |> filter(crowd == "Home arena, no fans")
bubble <- games |> filter(crowd == "Bubble (neutral, no fans)")

pt <- prop.test(x = c(sum(full$home_win), sum(nofans$home_win)),
                n = c(nrow(full), nrow(nofans)))
pt
```

```{r t-test}
tt <- t.test(full$margin, nofans$margin)   # Welch t-test by default (does not assume equal variances)
tt
```

```{r bubble-test}
# Bubble: is the home win rate significantly different from 50%?
binom.test(sum(bubble$home_win), nrow(bubble), p = 0.5)
```

The home win rate was `r scales::percent(mean(full$home_win), 0.1)` with a full crowd and
`r scales::percent(mean(nofans$home_win), 0.1)` in home arenas without fans
(p = `r signif(pt$p.value, 3)`). The average home margin fell from
`r round(mean(full$margin), 2)` to `r round(mean(nofans$margin), 2)` points
(p = `r signif(tt$p.value, 3)`).

Both p-values are well below 0.05, so we **reject H₀**: home teams did significantly worse
without fans. The difference is also meaningful in practice. A drop of about
`r round(100 * (mean(full$home_win) - mean(nofans$home_win)), 1)` percentage points means that,
without fans, the home team was barely more likely to win than a coin flip. In the bubble,
the home win rate was also not significantly different from 50%, which makes sense because
the "home" team was just a label there.

## Logistic regression

$$\log\frac{P(\text{home win})}{1-P(\text{home win})} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{crowd} + \beta_2\,\text{strength\_diff} + \beta_3\,\text{playoffs}$$

```{r logit}
logit <- glm(home_win ~ crowd + strength_diff + playoffs,
             data = games, family = binomial)
summary(logit)
```

Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals:

```{r logit-or}
tidy(logit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r logit-pred}
# Convert to probabilities: predicted home win % for two evenly matched teams
# (strength_diff = 0) in a regular-season game
newdata <- tibble(crowd = factor(levels(games$crowd), levels = levels(games$crowd)),
                  strength_diff = 0, playoffs = FALSE)
newdata |>
  mutate(pred_home_win = predict(logit, newdata, type = "response")) |>
  mutate(pred_home_win = scales::percent(pred_home_win, 0.1)) |>
  select(crowd, pred_home_win) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Crowd", "Predicted home win % (evenly matched teams)"))
```

```{r logit-numbers, include=FALSE}
or_tab <- tidy(logit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
or_nofans <- or_tab |> filter(term == "crowdHome arena, no fans")
or_bubble <- or_tab |> filter(term == "crowdBubble (neutral, no fans)")
or_strength_01 <- exp(0.1 * coef(logit)["strength_diff"])   # odds ratio per 0.1 increase in win% difference
```

Holding team strength and game type constant, the odds of a home win in a home arena
without fans were about **`r round(or_nofans$estimate, 2)` times** the odds with a full crowd
(95% CI: `r round(or_nofans$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(or_nofans$conf.high, 2)`). Since the
whole interval is below 1, the drop is statistically significant. The bubble estimate is
similar (OR = `r round(or_bubble$estimate, 2)`), but its interval includes 1 because there
were only `r nrow(bubble)` bubble games. Games with limited fans did not differ significantly
from full-crowd games, which suggests even a small crowd may be enough to restore some advantage.

Team strength is by far the strongest predictor. A 0.1 increase in `strength_diff` (for example,
a .600 team hosting a .500 team) multiplies the odds of a home win by about
`r round(or_strength_01, 2)`. Playoff games were not significantly different from regular-season games.

The prediction table makes this easier to read: for two evenly matched teams, the model
predicts the home team wins about 58% of the time with a full crowd, but only about 50%
in a home arena without fans, which is essentially no advantage at all.

## Linear regression on point margin

```{r lm}
lm_margin <- lm(margin ~ crowd + strength_diff + playoffs, data = games)
summary(lm_margin)
```

```{r lm-numbers, include=FALSE}
b <- coef(lm_margin)
```

The intercept (`r round(b["(Intercept)"], 2)`) means that when two evenly matched teams play
a regular-season game in front of a full crowd, the home team wins by about
`r round(b["(Intercept)"], 1)` points on average. Without fans in the home arena, this margin
drops by about `r round(-b["crowdHome arena, no fans"], 1)` points (p < 0.001), which wipes
out the home advantage almost completely. The bubble coefficient
(`r round(b["crowdBubble (neutral, no fans)"], 1)`) points the same way but is only borderline
significant (p ≈ 0.05). These results agree with the logistic model. Interestingly, playoff
games show a slightly larger home margin (about `r round(b["playoffsTRUE"], 1)` extra points),
even though the playoff effect on win probability was not significant.

The model's R² is only `r round(summary(lm_margin)$r.squared, 2)`, so most of the variation in
point margin is unexplained. This is expected: individual games depend on injuries, hot
shooting, and luck. Our goal is to estimate the crowd effect, not to predict single games.

## Model diagnostics

```{r diagnostics, fig.height = 7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(lm_margin)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r vif}
vif(lm_margin)   # GVIF^(1/(2*Df)) below ~2 means no serious multicollinearity
```

```{r logit-calibration}
# Calibration check: split predicted probabilities into 10 groups and
# compare predicted vs. observed home win rates
games |>
  mutate(pred = predict(logit, type = "response"),
         bin  = ntile(pred, 10)) |>
  group_by(bin) |>
  summarise(predicted = mean(pred), observed = mean(home_win)) |>
  ggplot(aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1d428a") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted P(home win)", y = "Observed home win rate",
       title = "Calibration of the logistic model (deciles)")
```

The residuals vs. fitted plot shows no clear pattern, so the linear form looks reasonable
and the variance is roughly constant. The Q-Q plot follows the line closely, with only slightly
heavier tails (a few blowout games), which is not a concern with over 14,000 observations.
No single game has high leverage. All VIF values are close to 1, so there is no
multicollinearity. For the logistic model, the calibration points lie almost exactly on the
diagonal, meaning the predicted probabilities match the observed win rates well.

One assumption that is not perfectly met is **independence**: games involving the same team
in the same season are related. This could make our standard errors a little too small, but
it is unlikely to change the main conclusion given how small the p-values are.

# Discussion

**1. Was the home win rate lower without fans?** Yes. Home teams won about 57% of games
with a full crowd but only about 50% in their own arena without fans. In other words,
home-court advantage did not just shrink; it basically disappeared.

**2. Does this hold after controlling for team strength?** Yes. Adding `strength_diff` and a
playoff indicator barely changed the result. Both the logistic and linear models show a
significant drop in home performance without fans, so the effect is not explained by
which teams happened to play at home.

**3. Does the home arena still help without fans?** Not really. Teams playing in their own
arena without fans did about as well as "home" teams in the neutral-site bubble. If travel
and arena familiarity were major factors, home teams without fans should have done clearly
better than bubble teams, but they did not. This points to **the crowd itself** as the main
source of home-court advantage, possibly through motivating players, distracting opponents,
or influencing referees.

That said, the pre-existing downward trend means part of the gap may not be caused by the
missing fans. Even compared with the post-COVID seasons (`r scales::percent(post_pct, 0.1)`
home wins), the no-fan games still show a drop of about 5 percentage points, so the crowd
effect appears to be real, just likely smaller than the raw comparison with all full-crowd
games suggests.

## Limitations

- **Not a randomized experiment.** The no-fan games happened during a pandemic, when
  schedules, rest, health protocols and player availability were all unusual.
- **Pre-existing trend.** Home win rates were already drifting down before COVID, so part of the
  difference may reflect a long-run trend rather than the absence of fans.
- **Team strength measure.** Season winning percentage includes the game being predicted and
  partly reflects home/away performance itself; a better control might use pre-game ratings or betting lines.
- **Attendance data quality.** Attendance is as reported by ESPN and may contain errors.
- **Small samples** for the bubble (`r nrow(bubble)` games) give wide confidence intervals.

- **Timing is confounded with crowd condition.** Most no-fan games happened early in the
  2020–21 season, and fans gradually returned later. Any changes over the season (e.g. teams
  adjusting to new protocols) are mixed in with the crowd effect.
- **Independence.** Games involving the same teams are not fully independent, which may
  make the standard errors slightly too small.

# Conclusion

Using more than 14,000 NBA games from 2015 to 2025, we found that home-court advantage
almost completely disappeared when games were played without fans. This result holds after
controlling for team strength, and home teams without fans performed about the same as
teams in the neutral-site bubble. Together, this suggests that crowds, rather than travel
or arena familiarity, drive most of the home-court advantage. However, home advantage was
already declining before COVID, so future work could use pre-game betting lines or a
longer time series to separate the crowd effect from this long-term trend.
